intro: Heidelberg protects seven designated trees, from a hollow, cable-strapped linden by the funicular's upper station to horse chestnuts on the way up to the castle and a pair of oaks above Ziegelhausen. Up in the city forest stand two more, a champion giant sequoia in the arboretum and a hollow, spiral-grown oak on the Heiligenberg, and a reader sent us a tall oak on a forest track above Schlierbach. The Molkenkur Linden comes closest, put at roughly 200 years by the local paper. All ten are free to visit, and eight of the ten pins are approximate.
meta_description: Heidelberg's ancient trees: a hollow, cable-strapped linden above the castle, horse chestnuts, a rare hybrid linden, oaks and more. All free.
question_meta: Heidelberg's best-documented old tree is the Molkenkur Linden above the castle, put at roughly 200 years by the local paper. Where it stands.
question_answer: The closest thing to a documented age among Heidelberg's designated trees belongs to the Molkenkur Linden, hollow inside and held together with cables, put at roughly 200 years by the Rhein-Neckar-Zeitung. It stands at the Molkenkur viewpoint above Heidelberg Castle. The other six designated trees on this page carry no recorded age at all, only the date they were designated a natural monument.
question_context: The 200-year figure for the Molkenkur Linden comes from a newspaper feature rather than a growth-rate reading or a ring count, and this page carries it as a loose middle point, 150 to 250 years, rather than a precise number. The trunk is genuinely hollow, and the crown has been held together with steel cables for twenty years, a maintenance choice the city has committed to rather than felling it. Nothing else here has comparable evidence. The Schlossberg Beech, the Neuenheimer Landstrasse Swamp Cypress, the Zwingerstrasse Horse Chestnuts, the Bergstrasse Crimean Linden, the Ringstrasse Oak and the Münchelstrasse Oaks are each documented only by a state register entry giving a name, a coordinate and a designation date between 1939 and 1986, with no age, girth or description. Six of the seven register pins come from its own coordinate rather than a reading at the trunk, hence approximate. Two forest trees sit outside the register. Two tree registers estimate the Arboretum Giant Sequoia's planting at around 1876, and the Holdermann Oak has no recorded age at all. If you can measure or place any of them more precisely, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Heidelberg?
faq.a: The Molkenkur Linden above the castle is the best-documented, put at roughly 200 years by the local paper. The other six designated trees here carry no recorded age at all.

faq.q: Why is the Molkenkur Linden hollow?
faq.a: Age and decay rather than damage. The trunk is empty but the tree is described as completely vital, and its crown has been held together with steel cables for the last twenty years so it can keep standing.

faq.q: Are the pins for these trees exact?
faq.a: Eight of the ten are approximate, so expect the right street, garden or stretch of forest path rather than the exact spot.

faq.q: Are these trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. Six stand on open public ground: a viewpoint, a castle garden, streets and a tram stop. The Münchelstrasse oaks stand on or beside a public forest track above Ziegelhausen; keep to the track. The arboretum sequoia, the Holdermann Oak and the oak on the Drachenhöhlenweg are on open paths in the city forest. No ticket needed for any of them, though the castle courtyard itself is separately ticketed.

trees.name: The Molkenkur Linden

location.address: Molkenkur, Heidelberg (below the Schlosshotel Molkenkur, on the Königstuhl slope above the castle)

trees.story:
Hollow inside and completely vital. That is the local paper's verdict on this linden, and the two halves of it are both true. The trunk is empty, the tree is in no trouble, and for the last twenty years its crown has been held together with cables so that it stays that way. The city has no intention of felling it.

It stands at the Molkenkur, the shoulder of the Königstuhl directly above Heidelberg Castle, where the funicular makes its stop and where people come for one of Heidelberg's best-known views. The linden has been a protected natural monument since October 1958, so it has spent the whole postwar life of the city on a register.

Its age is given as roughly two hundred years by the newspaper that wrote it up, and nobody has done better than that. No ring count, no girth measurement, and the register does not even settle which linden it is, large-leaved or small-leaved. Treat two hundred as the middle of a wide band rather than a fact.

One thing to know before you climb. Our pin comes from the register's map tile rather than a reading taken at the trunk, so it puts you in the right place at the Molkenkur and not on the exact spot. Look for the cables, because a hollow veteran wearing steel is not hard to pick out.
trees.access: Free, public viewpoint area at Molkenkur; no ticket needed to reach or stand by the tree.
trees.transport: Heidelberg funicular (Bergbahn) from Kornmarkt to the Molkenkur stop, a few minutes; also reachable on foot via the Klingentor path from the castle, roughly 15-20 minutes uphill.

photo.attribution: Hartmut Schmidt Heidelberg, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its hollow trunk and cabled crown, standing at the viewpoint where the funicular stops above Heidelberg Castle. It stands at the Molkenkur, on the Konigstuhl slope.

best_time.label: late June, when the Molkenkur linden flowers above the castle, scented and loud with bees

trees.name: The Schlossberg Beech

location.address: Schlossberg, in the Heidelberg Schlossgarten (castle garden), below/around the castle terraces

trees.story:
This beech was made a protected natural monument on 17 November 1939, ten weeks into the war, which is a curious moment to be filing paperwork about a tree. The register entry reads simply Rotbuche Schlossberg, red beech on the castle hill, and it has carried that one line ever since without acquiring a further sentence of description.

That is the honest problem with this one. The state register confirms the designation, the name and the coordinate, and then stops: no age, no girth, not a word of text, its own file noting that no document exists for the object. A separate piece on beeches in the state's castle gardens describes fourteen mature red beeches at the Scheffelterrasse, on the edge of this same garden, which tells you old beeches genuinely grow here but does not pick out the designated one. So we can send you to the right corner of the Schlossgarten and not to the exact trunk.

It is worth the walk anyway, because the setting does the work. The Schlossgarten is the terraced garden below Heidelberg Castle, free and open in daylight, and a mature European beech there is standing in ground that has been laid out, ruined and replanted more than once since the castle above it was still a palace. Grey trunk, smooth bark, a canopy that keeps the ground beneath it bare.

If you can tell which beech carries the designation, we would like to know.
trees.access: Free. The Schlossgarten (castle garden and terraces) is open to the public daily in daylight hours at no charge; only the castle courtyard itself, the Grosses Fass and the Apothecary Museum need the paid Schlossticket.
trees.transport: Short uphill walk from Kornmarkt via Kurzer Buckel, or the Bergbahn funicular from Kornmarkt to the Schloss stop.

best_time.label: October to November: copper and russet, and young trees keep dead leaves all winter

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the smooth grey trunk and the bare ground a beech keeps beneath it. Which of the Schlossgarten's mature beeches carries the 1939 designation is not recorded, so it stands somewhere on these terraces.

trees.name: The Neuenheimer Landstrasse Swamp Cypress

location.address: Neuenheimer Landstrasse, Neuenheim, along the north bank of the Neckar

trees.story:
A tree from the swamps of the American southeast has been protected on a Heidelberg riverside road since 28 July 1942. The register calls it Sumpfzypresse Neuenheimer Landstrasse and gives nothing else: no age, no girth, no description. The designation itself is the whole record, and it is a long one, because eighty-four years of protection on a public road is not nothing.

Bald cypress is the conifer that behaves like a broadleaf. It grows in standing water in Louisiana and the Carolinas, throws up woody knees from its roots when the ground is wet, and drops every needle each winter after turning a deep rust orange. A specimen doing that on the north bank of the Neckar, in a line of ordinary street trees, is a peculiar and rather good thing to come across.

Two honest notes. The register does not print a binomial, so the species here is the reading that German registers almost always mean by Sumpfzypresse; if you can tell a true bald cypress from a pond cypress on the ground, we would like your verdict. And our pin is the register's own coordinate rather than a fix taken at the trunk, so it puts you on the right stretch of the Neuenheimer Landstrasse rather than at the tree.

Do not confuse it with the swamp cypresses at the Tertiärgärtchen in the Neuenheimer Feld. Different site, several hundred metres away.
trees.access: Free. A street tree on Neuenheimer Landstrasse, a public riverside road with a pavement/cycle path; viewable at any time.
trees.transport: Short walk along the Neckar's north bank from the Alte Bruecke (Old Bridge), Neuenheim side; also served by Neuenheim bus and tram stops.

best_time.label: November, when the needles turn rust orange before dropping

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the conifer that goes rust orange and then bare in winter, in a line of otherwise ordinary street trees. It stands on the Neuenheimer Landstrasse along the north bank of the Neckar, not at the Tertiärgärtchen.

trees.name: The Zwingerstrasse Horse Chestnuts

location.address: Zwingerstrasse, Altstadt, between Kettengasse and Burgweg, near the funicular's Talstation

trees.story:
Heidelberg protects a whole small stand of horse chestnuts here as one object, not a single trunk. The register lists them as Rosskastanien Zwingerstrasse, designated on 3 February 1986, and treats the group as the thing worth keeping. Stand at the corner of the Zwingerstrasse and you take them in at once, which is exactly why they were listed together.

They stand a couple of minutes from the Kornmarkt and the bottom station of the castle funicular, on the strip of street that runs under the Schlossberg. Almost everyone who walks up to the castle from the old town passes them, which is the modest sort of witnessing an urban tree does: not events, but everybody.

The horse chestnut is not native to Germany either. It came out of the Balkan mountains and spread across Europe through beer gardens and avenues, planted for the dense shade it throws. In early May the flower spikes go up like candles all over the crown, white with a yellow throat that turns red once the flower has been pollinated, which is the tree telling the bees not to bother twice. In autumn the conkers come down on the pavement.

Neither the register nor anything else we found gives an age or a girth for these trees, and the coordinate is the register's own rather than a reading taken under them. If you know how old they are, tell us.
trees.access: Free. Zwingerstrasse is an ordinary public street in the Altstadt, a few minutes' walk from Kornmarkt and the Bergbahn funicular's lower station.
trees.transport: A few minutes' walk from Kornmarkt or the Bergbahn Talstation.

best_time.label: early May, when the flower spikes stand up like candles across the whole crown

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as a stand rather than a single trunk, listed as one object, with white May candles whose yellow throats turn red once pollinated. They stand on Zwingerstrasse, near the funicular's lower station.

trees.name: The Bergstrasse Crimean Linden
trees.story:
A Crimean linden is a garden hybrid. Tilia x euchlora appeared in cultivation around 1860, a cross of the small-leaved linden with a Caucasian relative, and it was planted across Europe for one reason: its leaves are glossy dark green and it shrugs off city air better than its parents. That is the tree standing on the Bergstrasse in Neuenheim, and Heidelberg has protected it as a natural monument since 4 August 1986.

Which makes the designation the interesting part. Registers usually protect trees for being old, and a hybrid that first appeared around 1860 gives no specimen anywhere much more than a century and a half to work with. Something about this particular specimen persuaded the state to list it, and the register does not say what: it gives the name, Krimlinde Bergstrasse, the date and the coordinate, and then nothing at all. No age, no girth, no description.

So this is a tree to go and judge for yourself, on a quiet residential street on the north side of the Neckar, and to tell us about. How thick is it? How tall? The species usually tops out around 15 to 18 metres, and if this one is well past that you are looking at one of the larger ones anywhere.

Our pin is the register's coordinate rather than a fix at the trunk, so expect the right stretch of pavement rather than the exact spot. A second monument, two cypresses, sits at almost the same point.
trees.access: Free. Bergstrasse is an ordinary public residential street in Neuenheim; the tree stands as a street tree, viewable from the pavement.
trees.transport: A short walk from Neuenheim's Bergstrasse/Blumenthalstrasse bus stops.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the glossy dark green leaves of a Crimean linden, a species that usually tops out around 15 to 18 metres. It stands on the Bergstrasse in Neuenheim, at almost the same point as two protected cypresses.

trees.name: The Ringstrasse Oak

location.address: Ringstrasse, near the Ringstrasse tram stop, Kirchheim/Bahnstadt

trees.story:
The register calls this one simply Eiche, oak, and that omission is deliberate rather than sloppy. The same list names three other Heidelberg oaks precisely as Stieleiche, pedunculate oak, so when it declines to do so here it is telling us that nobody established which oak this is. We have kept it that way rather than tidying it up. Go and look: a pedunculate oak hangs its acorns on long stalks and has almost no leaf stalk, a sessile oak does the exact opposite. Whichever you find, tell us, and the page changes.

It has been a protected natural monument since 14 October 1958, standing on the Ringstrasse where the number 26 tram stops, on the border between Kirchheim and the Bahnstadt. The Bahnstadt beside it has since been rebuilt from a railway goods yard into a residential district, so the ground on one side of this oak is entirely new.

Nothing has ever been published about its age or its girth, and the pin comes from the register's coordinate rather than a reading at the trunk, so aim for the tram stop and look around.

It sits a good two kilometres from the old town, so treat it as its own short trip rather than a stop on a castle walk.
trees.access: Free. Ringstrasse is a public street served by tram line 26 (Ringstrasse stop); the tree is a street tree, viewable at any time.
trees.transport: Tram line 26 to the Ringstrasse stop, then on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the oak the register would not name: look at whether the acorns hang on long stalks and the leaves on almost none, then tell us. It stands by the Ringstrasse tram stop on line 26.

trees.name: The Münchelstrasse Oaks
trees.story:
On 5 April 1951 two pedunculate oaks on Münchelstrasse were made natural monuments on the same day, together with a lime a little further along the same track. Seventy-five years later all three are still in the register, and both oaks were photographed standing in November 2024.

Münchelstrasse is not a town street but a forest track climbing above Ziegelhausen, the Heidelberg district on the Neckar east of the old town. The oaks are registered separately, as Münchelstrasse (1) and (2), about 70 metres apart, so this is a short walk between two trunks rather than a single stop. The lime, Linde Münchelstrasse, stands roughly 50 metres beyond the second oak.

That is close to everything on the record. The Baden-Württemberg register gives the names, the species and the date, and no girth, no height and no age. We have found no other source that does better, and we will not guess. A protection order in 1951 says somebody thought them worth keeping then; how old they already were, nobody wrote down. If you have put a tape round either trunk, or know why these two were singled out, tell us.

Our pins are approximate, so expect to look around once you are on the track. We have not confirmed whether the ground at their feet is public, so stay on the path.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the two oaks on the Münchelstrasse forest track above Ziegelhausen, about 70 metres apart. A registered lime stands some 50 metres further along the same track.

official_register.name: Naturdenkmal Stieleiche Münchelstraße (1) and (2), LUBW Baden-Württemberg, protected 1951-04-05, no. 82210001208, 82210001209

trees.access: Stands on or beside Münchelstrasse, mapped in OpenStreetMap as a public track (highway=track, no access restriction seen). No source states opening conditions; evidence only.
trees.transport: Ziegelhausen, Heidelberg; bus to Ziegelhausen then an uphill walk on Münchelstrasse (exact stop and time not verified).

trees.name: The Arboretum Giant Sequoia

location.address: Arboretum 1, Sprunghöhe, Heidelberg city forest (69117 / 69115), reached from the forest car park on Klingenteichstraße towards Gaiberg

trees.story:
The ring of wooden logs around this tree's foot is not its own size. It marks the girth of the General Sherman Tree in California, about 31 metres round, laid out on the forest floor so you can hold the Heidelberg sequoia up against its most famous relative.

The Heidelberg one holds up well for a newcomer. It is the strongest giant sequoia in Arboretum 1 on the Sprunghöhe, and the German Dendrology Society lists it among the country's champion trees, at 7.92 metres round in 2021. A Baumkunde visit in September 2025 measured 7.65 metres and a height of 35; the society's estimate is nearer 40. Two tapes, two numbers, so call it about 7.7 to 7.9 metres.

Its planting is estimated at around 1876. That is also the year Heidelberg's head forester decided to start planting non-native trees in the city forest, which is why these slopes hold so many exotics. Treat the date as an estimate for this trunk rather than a record, so roughly 150 years.

The arboretum around it is themed on North America, with a bench carrying a totem pole and a table shaped like a bald eagle along the circular path. The city calls the giant redwood one of the most awe-inspiring trees in its forest. A reader sent it to us, and the society last recorded it as fully vital.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the thickest giant sequoia in Arboretum 1, about 7.7 metres round. It stands inside a ring of wooden logs laid out to show the girth of the General Sherman Tree.
trees.access: Free, open forest walk in the Heidelberg city forest. The Arboretum 1 circular path starts at the forest car park beside a log cabin on the road from Klingenteichstrasse towards Gaiberg, past a rhododendron garden.

official_register.name: Deutsche Dendrologische Gesellschaft, Liste der Rekordbäume (Champion Trees), ID 7000, rank DE 16, BW 11

trees.pin_source: OSM natural=tree node 1129572660 (49.4003654, 8.7096497), which carries the DDG, Baumkunde and Monumentaltrees refs for this tree; Baumkunde's own coordinate (N49°24.008' E8°42.585' = 49.40013, 8.70975) lies about 25 m away, and the arboretum's other giant sequoias stand within 100 m, so kept approximate

trees.name: The Holdermann Oak
trees.age_estimate: not documented, centuries old by reputation

location.address: Heiligenberg forest above Handschuhsheim / Ziegelhausen, Heidelberg (forest path, no street address)

trees.story:
Prussian troops and the Volkswehr fought a skirmish at this oak on 21 June 1849, according to a Heidelberg local history of the fortifications on the Heiligenberg. The oak is the landmark the report uses to say where the shooting was.

The name is older gossip. It belongs to Friedrich Holdermann, a wealthy Heidelberg innkeeper who owned the White Bear in Kettengasse, a beer house and a coffee house. A story repeated by walkers says he shot himself at the oak in 1764. We have found it only in that retelling, never in a record, so take it as the forest's version rather than history.

What stands there now is a hollow oak whose trunk grew in a spiral, at a junction of paths in the city forest above Handschuhsheim, with one of Heidelberg's signpost stones beside it. Walkers describe the cavity, and mapping volunteers tag it as a natural monument, though we have not found its entry in the city's register.

That entry would tell us the rest. Nobody we can find has published its girth, its age or even which species of oak it is, so its centuries are a local reputation rather than a measurement. A reader sent it to us. If you have put a tape round it, or know its register number, tell us and we will add it.

The forest paths up the Heiligenberg get slippery after rain.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the hollow trunk, grown in a spiral. It stands at a junction of forest paths on the Heiligenberg above Handschuhsheim, beside a Heidelberg signpost stone.
trees.access: Free, on open public paths in the Heidelberg city forest (Naturpark Neckartal-Odenwald), about 1.4 km along the climb from Handschuhsheim to the Heiligenberg. Paths can be slippery after rain.
trees.pin_source: OSM natural=tree node 1879169245 'Holdermannseiche' (49.4313408, 8.7196703), tagged denotation=natural_monument and monument=yes, with a note citing the city's Wegweiserstein (signpost stone) list; the reader's Google place 'Holdermanns-Eiche, 69121' carries no coordinate in its link
trees.verify_notes: 2026-11-20 verify and write: reader's tip 1063. Flagged, thin: no official register entry, no girth, age or species found. Existence from three independent mentions: OSM node 1879169245 (denotation=natural_monument, note citing the city's signpost stone list), komoot highlight 142249 and tour 29264, and a regional history PDF (BLB Karlsruhe) placing a skirmish between Prussian troops and the Volkswehr at the Holdermannseiche on 1849-06-21. The 1764 suicide anecdote comes from a komoot user and is told on the page as a retelling. Alive: lifecheck RECENT 2026-04-26 (iNaturalist near the pin, not confirmed to be this trunk); komoot 2017-18 describe the hollow spiral trunk. Species left as genus. Pin approximate (OSM node).

trees.name: The Oak on the Drachenhöhlenweg
trees.age_estimate: about 200 years, by a reader's estimate

location.address: Mittlerer Drachenhöhlenweg, city forest above Schlierbach, Heidelberg

trees.how_to_recognise: Beside the forest track: a single tall oak with a dark, straight trunk rising clear of the beeches around it, a small sign on a post at its foot.
trees.access: Free, beside a forest track in the Heidelberg city forest above Schlierbach. Stout shoes after rain.
trees.story:
A reader walking the forest above Schlierbach, on Heidelberg's eastern edge, stopped at this oak on the Mittlerer Drachenhöhlenweg in November and sent us its photograph.

It is the kind of tree a forest keeps when it lets the rest come and go. Beeches crowd in on both sides of the track, their leaves gone copper, and the oak rises through them on a dark, straight trunk that runs clear for a long way before it opens into a high crown of crooked black limbs, still holding a scatter of brown leaves against the blue sky. At its foot a small sign stands on a post, so someone has thought it worth marking.

The reader puts it at about 200 years. That figure is theirs; we have no girth, no register entry and no written record of it yet, and we do not know which oak it is, pedunculate or sessile. If you can read the sign, measure the trunk or tell the two oaks apart by the acorn stalks, tell us here and we will add it.

Walk on past it a little way and look back, where the trunk stands clearest against the beeches.

pin_source.note: The pin marks where a reader stood to photograph this tree; the photograph was checked to show it.
